answer.answer: Gross margin is not a relevant metric for JPMorgan Chase, so I can't say whether it stayed within roughly 2% each year. As a bank, JPM has no cost of goods sold and reports no gross profit. Its income statement shows noninterest revenue plus net interest income (interest income minus interest expense, for example $66,710M in 2022, $52,311M in 2021 and $54,563M in 2020), then provision for credit losses and noninterest expense. Better measures for a bank are net interest margin, the efficiency (overhead) ratio, ROE/ROTCE and credit costs.

answer.answer: Gross margin isn't a useful metric for American Express. It is a card issuer and payments network, so it has no cost of goods sold or cost of revenue line and reports 'total revenues net of interest expense' instead. The closest measure is how much of its interest income it keeps: in FY2022 interest expense took 21.8% of interest income ($2,763M of $12,658M), up from 14.2% in FY2021, because it paid higher rates on deposits and debt. Even so, net interest income rose 28% to $9,895M on larger loan balances and higher rates, and total revenues net of interest expense rose 25% to $52,862M, mainly because Card Member spending lifted discount revenue 25% to $30,739M, while profit was held back by credit-loss provisions of $2,182M (a $1,419M release in 2021) and higher rewards, marketing and operating costs.

answer.answer: At the end of Q2 FY2023 (December 31, 2022), Amcor's restructuring liability was $93 million, down from $118 million on June 30, 2022.
